newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says finds 30,000 Iraqi Kurd refugees in Iran.
newsitem.headline: UN says finds 30,000 Iraqi Kurd refugees in Iran.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Saturday an inspection team had so far found about 30,000 Kurdish refugees from recent fighting in Iraq in camps on the Iranian side of the border.

Spokeswoman Judith Melby said the team, sent to assess the needs of the refugees under an emergency UNHCR operation, had been impressed with arrangements made by the Iranian Red Crescent society in setting up the camps.

Citing the UNHCR representative in Tehran, Roger Vivarie, she said the group had visited four of the five camps where the Iranian authorities say there are a total of around 40,000 people from northern and western areas of Iraq.
"We think that total is about right," said Melby.
The UNHCR has assigned $3.6 million from its emergency fund to provide shelter, food and medicines for the refugees.

In camps in three Iranian areas bordering on northern Iraq, some refugees had brought with them some of their own supplies and cooking equipment and appeared to be in relatively good health, the team reported.

Iraqi Kurds in these areas -- Sardasht, Cyramband and Baghmagh -- fled into Iran after a one of the two major Kurdish factions took control of most of northern Iraq over the past two weeks with backing from the Baghdad government.
But Vivarie reported that Kurds in a camp in Iran's Kermanshah province which borders an area of Iraq always under government control appeared in much worse physical shape.

Melby quoted him as saying they were showing signs of the effects of the five-year international economic sanctions imposed on Iraq in the wake of its brief seizure of Kuwait in 1990. Many of them were now returning to Iraq.
It was not immediately clear why Kurds from this area -- where there had been no fighting between Kurdish factions -- had crossed into Iran.
But some may have feared bombing by the United States in retaliation for President Sadam Hussein's activities in the Kurdish "safe haven" areas in the north, the spokeswoman said.

On Friday, UNHCR spokesman Rupert Colville said most of the Kurds who had managed to cross into Iran -- negotiating Iraqi minefields on the way -- were sleeping in the open, due to a serious shortage of tents.
The spokesman described the situation as fluid, adding: "People are still coming in across the border but there has been quite a big return movement taking place, too."
On Wednesday, Iran said it was sheltering 39,000 Kurdish refugees and said it needed international assistance to cope.
Colville said some cases of flu and diarrhoea have been reported among the refugees in Sardasht, but Iranian medical teams were circulating among them.
The Iranian Red Crescent had distributed bread, potatoes, rice and biscuits in Sardasht, "but they don't have sufficient quantities at present", according to the UNHCR spokesman.
UNHCR has praised Tehran's track record in giving asylum to millions of desperate refugees from Afghanistan and Iraq starting in the 1980s.
Iran is currently home to two million refugees, 1.4 million from Afghanistan and 600,000 from Iraq -- making it the largest host country in the world, according to UNHCR.
